study.title: Exodus 34 The renewal of the covenant, the revelation of the name of the LORD, and the shining face of Moses
study.overview: The chapter shows the Lord restoring the covenant after the sin of the golden calf. First, He commands Moses to rise again to Sinai with new tables, and then reveals his name and character: merciful, godly, patient and righteous. Then he reaffirms the demands of the covenant, especially the exclusivity of worship, the separation of idolatrous practices and the observance of the central feasts and commandments. Finally, the text closes with Moses descending from the mountain with his shining face, a visible sign that he was in the presence of God, which provokes fear in the people and demands the use of a veil when Moses speaks publicly.

outline.title: New boards and new climb to Sinai
outline.explanation: The LORD sends Moses to prepare two tablets similar to the first and to climb to the mountain alone. The scene indicates resumption after the breakup of the previous covenant: the people failed, but God orders the continuity of the covenant relationship under his initiative and authority.

outline.title: The proclamation of the name of the LORD and the intercession of Moses
outline.explanation: God descends into the cloud and proclaims his name, that is, his identity and his way of acting. The text highlights his mercy, faithfulness and justice. Moses responds with worship and asks God to remain with the people, forgiving them and taking him as his property.

outline.title: Renewed alliance terms: exclusivity, worship and memory
outline.explanation: The Lord promises to act powerfully for the people, but insists on obedience. He forbids alliances with the peoples of the earth, orders to destroy idolatrous altars, forbids fused images and reaffirms practices such as the feast of unleavened loaves, the dedication of the firstborn, the Sabbath, the feast of weeks and the offerings of the firstfruits. At the end, the period of forty days and nights in which the covenant is written on the boards is recorded.

outline.title: The face of Moses and the veil
outline.explanation: As he descended from the mountain, Moses reflects the glory of the conversation with God, without immediately realizing. The people fear to come near, and Moses goes on to wear a veil in speaking to them, withdrawing them when he enters before the LORD. The episode communicates the honor of Moses as a mediator and the visible reality of divine proximity.

study.context: The chapter presupposes the former sin of the golden calf and the need for the restoration of the covenant. The setting is Mount Sinai, where Moses acts as a mediator between God and Israel. The instructions resume and reinforce commitments already given to the people, especially the demands of exclusivity in the worship and separation of idolatrous practices of the surrounding nations. The text also places Israel as the newly freed people of Egypt and called to live by memory, worship, and obedience.
study.theology: Exodus 34 unites grace and holiness. God is presented as the one who restores the covenant on his own initiative, even though the people have broken it. His self-declaration emphasizes mercy, longsuffering, kindness, and truth, but without erasing his righteousness: He forgives, but he does not treat evil as indifferent. The renewal of the alliance requires exclusivity: there is no space for mixed worship, alliances with idolatry or fused images. The feasts, the sabbath and the dedication of the first fruits and firstborn teach that every life belongs to the Lord. The resplendent face of Moses points to the seriousness of mediation and to the effect of the divine presence upon those who contemplate it in a special way. In evangelical reading, the chapter prepares the understanding that God is at the same time reconciling and holy, and that his presence transforms and separates a people for himself.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter shows the renewal of the covenant as God's unilateral initiative, which reaffirms its fidelity to the people despite the previous break of the covenant.
The prohibition of alliances with the peoples of the earth and the order to destroy their altars show that the restoration of communion with God requires a decided departure from idolatry.
The shining face of Moses is presented as a sign of the glory of the relationship with God and as a practical reason for the use of the veil before the people.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the difference between God's forgiveness and tolerance to sin?
What practices today work as dangerous alliances with idolatry, even without casting images?
How should God's presence transform our way of speaking, worshiping and living publicly?
study.practice: Read the chapter as called to renewal: confess where there was a breach of fidelity, return to the basics of obedience and exclusive worship, and set aside concrete time to remember that all that you have belongs to the Lord. Also look for signs of mixed commitments in your life - values, habits, or relationships that weaken your devotion - and treat them seriously. The presence of God is not only comforting; it also reorders priorities and leaves visible marks.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text, in this translation, presents a small tension in 34:27-28 about who wrote the words on the tablets; the notes recognize this difficulty and mention different interpretive possibilities. In addition, the provided notes do not develop in detail all the rites and parties mentioned, so the historical and liturgical synthesis was maintained only at the level explicitly supported by the chapter and the comments given.
